mainTopic: Dangerous foods, the snake-bitten deer, and the signs of kosher animals, birds, grasshoppers and fish
overview: The amud opens by finishing a plant definition and bringing health warnings. רב יהודה and רבי אבהו warn about eating חלתית on an empty stomach, and רב יוסף warns about a heavy mix of foods eaten in summer. Next comes a story about a deer brought to the ריש גלותא. רב checked it and found it kosher, but שמואל worried it had been bitten by a snake. An oven test proved him right. A new משנה then teaches that the Torah gives the kosher signs for בהמה and חיה, while חכמים gave signs for birds and grasshoppers, and fish need fins and scales. The גמרא explains a ברייתא about teeth: an animal with no upper front teeth is kosher. רב חסדא gives three backup tests for an animal whose signs are damaged: teeth, hooves, and flesh. For each test he names the one exception to watch for: the young camel, the חזיר, and the ערוד. Finally the גמרא asks why a חיה needs its own signs, and רבי זירא's answer begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: It is the root of a bitter plant
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes identifying a plant from the discussion just before: it is the root of a bitter plant.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the root of a bitter plant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an explanation that started on the previous page by telling us what a certain plant is: the root of a bitter plant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line answers a 'what is it?' question from just before. It only defines the plant. It does not add any new law, and the next lines build on this plant topic.

phrases.english: It is the root of a bitter plant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a definition that began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plant is the root of a bitter plant.

steps.title: Eating three shekels of asafoetida on an empty stomach
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה warns that eating three shekels' weight of חלתית on an empty stomach makes a person's skin peel off.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says: Someone who eats three shekels of asafoetida on an empty stomach, his skin peels off.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a health warning: a large amount of חלתית eaten on an empty stomach is dangerous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger depends on two things together: the amount (three shekels' weight) and an empty stomach. The result is that the person's skin peels.

keyTerms.meaning: a shekel, used here as a measure of weight
asafoetida, a strong, sharp plant resin
literally 'on an empty heart'; on an empty stomach

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says:
This one who eats
three shekels of asafoetida
phrases.notes: Shekels here are a weight, not money.

phrases.english: on an empty heart,
phrases.notes: 'Empty heart' just means an empty stomach.

phrases.english: his skin peels off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הַאי מַאן דַּאֲכַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defining a plant to warning about a dangerous plant.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three shekels of חלתית on an empty stomach make a person's skin peel.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's own close call with asafoetida
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו tells how he ate even one shekel of חלתית and was saved only by sitting in water. He applies the פסוק 'wisdom gives life to those who have it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: It happened to me. I ate one shekel of asafoetida, and if I had not sat in water, my skin would have peeled. I fulfilled in myself the verse 'Wisdom preserves the life of the one who has it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו backs up רב יהודה's warning with a real event from his own life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His story shows that even one shekel, less than רב יהודה's three, was dangerous. He was saved only because he knew to cool himself in water. That is why he quotes the פסוק about wisdom saving a life.

keyTerms.meaning: an incident or event that actually happened
wisdom gives life to the one who has it

phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said:
There was an incident with me,
and I ate one shekel of asafoetida,
and had I not sat in water,
my skin would have peeled off,
and I fulfilled in myself
"Wisdom preserves the life of the one who has it."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: בְּדִידִי הֲוָה עוֹבָדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב יהודה's warning with a personal story.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's warning that חלתית on an empty stomach is dangerous
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבהו's own experience: even one shekel almost made his skin peel

steps.title: A dangerous mix of foods in the summer
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף warns that eating sixteen eggs, forty nuts, seven caper fruits and a quarter-log of honey in summer on an empty stomach damages the heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף says: Someone who eats sixteen eggs, forty nuts and seven caper fruits, and drinks a quarter-log of honey in the season of תמוז, on an empty stomach, his heartstrings are torn out.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds another warning about a dangerous way of eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of warning as before, but with a large combination of foods. The danger comes from eating them together, in the hot season of תמוז, on an empty stomach. The result is serious harm to the heart.

keyTerms.meaning: the 'hangers' of his heart; his heartstrings

phrases.english: Rav Yosef says:
This one who eats sixteen eggs,
and forty nuts,
and seven fruits of the caper bush,
and drinks a quarter-log of honey
in the season of Tammuz,
on an empty heart,
his heartstrings are torn out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: הַאי מַאן דְּאָכֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, similar warning about eating on an empty stomach.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This heavy mix of foods, eaten in summer on an empty stomach, causes serious damage to the heart.
steps.whatToRemember: These warnings all share the phrase אַלִּיבָּא רֵיקָנָא. An empty stomach is what makes these foods dangerous.

steps.title: רב checks a deer with cut legs and declares it kosher
steps.stepSummary: A slaughtered young deer with cut hind legs is brought to the ריש גלותא. רב checks the place where the leg sinews meet, declares it kosher, and plans to eat it rare.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain young deer came to the house of the ריש גלותא, and its hind legs had been cut. רב checked it at the meeting point of the sinews and declared it kosher. He planned to eat from it lightly roasted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's topic of an animal bitten by a snake by telling a story. This step sets up the scene for שמואל's question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deer's legs were damaged, so רב checked the key spot in the leg where cut sinews would make it a טרפה. He found it fine and declared it kosher. He then wanted to eat it rare, and that is what will draw a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: the Exilarch, leader of the Jews in Babylonia
the meeting point of the sinews in the leg

phrases.english: A certain young deer
that came to the house of the Exilarch,
whose hind legs had been cut,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Either way, the meaning is the same.

phrases.english: Rav checked it at the meeting point of the sinews
and declared it kosher.
He planned to eat from it lightly roasted.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא בַּר טַבְיָא דַּאֲתָא לְבֵי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the health warnings and returns to the משנה's rule about an animal bitten by a snake.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב found the sinews in the deer's leg intact and declared the deer kosher.

steps.title: שמואל asks: what about a snakebite?
steps.stepSummary: שמואל challenges רב: even if the deer is kosher, should he not worry that it was bitten by a snake before eating it rare?
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said to him: Is the Master not worried about a snakebite?
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל questions רב's plan to eat the deer rare, raising the worry that it may have been bitten by a snake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל does not argue with רב's ruling that the deer is kosher. His point is about danger: the משנה says a snake-bitten animal is not a טרפה, but it is still forbidden because of the danger. Eating it rare could be risky.

keyTerms.meaning: bites, here meaning a snake's bite

steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the deer is a טרפה. A snakebite does not make an animal a טרפה. The worry is only about the danger to the person eating it.

phrases.english: Shmuel said to him:
Is the Master not concerned about a snakebite?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל: לָא חָיֵישׁ מָר לְנִיקּוּרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's plan to eat the deer rare.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's plan to eat the deer lightly roasted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Checking the sinews shows the deer is not a טרפה, but it does not rule out a snakebite. A snakebite brings danger, and eating the meat rare could be harmful.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that being kosher and being safe are two separate questions. A kosher animal can still be forbidden because of danger.

steps.title: רב asks how to fix the worry
steps.stepSummary: רב asks שמואל how to deal with the worry that a snake bit the deer.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What is the fix?
steps.whatsHappening: רב accepts שמואל's worry and asks what can be done about it. This sets up שמואל's practical answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב does not argue against the snake worry from step 6. He moves straight to asking for a practical test, so the conversation shifts from 'is there a problem?' to 'how do we check?'

keyTerms.meaning: a fix, a remedy, a way to solve a problem

phrases.english: He said to him: What is the fix?
phrases.notes: רב is the one asking here, and he is speaking to שמואל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to שמואל's snake concern by asking for a practical solution.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical way to find out whether the deer was bitten by a snake.

steps.title: שמואל suggests the oven test
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says to put the meat in a hot oven, because the oven will show whether there is a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us put it in the oven, since it will check itself.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers רב's question. He suggests putting the meat in a hot oven so the meat will 'test itself.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A snake bite cannot be seen just by looking at the meat. The heat of the oven brings out the hidden damage, so the meat itself becomes the test.

keyTerms.meaning: it checks itself, it reveals its own condition

phrases.english: Let us put it in the oven,
phrases.notes: שמואל is the one answering now, even though the text doesn't say his name.

phrases.english: since it will check itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב's question from step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Put the meat in a hot oven; if it was bitten by a snake, the heat will show it.

steps.title: The meat falls apart, showing a snake bite
steps.stepSummary: שמואל puts the meat in the oven, and it falls apart into pieces. This shows a snake really had bitten the deer.
steps.simpleTranslation: He put it in, and it fell apart, piece by piece.
steps.whatsHappening: The test is carried out, and the meat falls apart in bits. This shows שמואל's worry was correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The meat falling apart is the proof that the snake had bitten the deer. So רב was right that the deer was kosher by its signs, and שמואל was right that there was still a hidden danger to eating it.

phrases.english: He put it in, and it fell apart, piece by piece.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the oven test from step 8 and shows what happened.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's worry that the deer had been bitten by a snake.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The meat fell apart in the oven.

steps.title: Each sage praises the other with a verse
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says a פסוק about רב, that no harm comes to a צדיק. רב says a פסוק about שמואל, that no secret is too hard for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said about רב: 'No harm will happen to the righteous.' רב said about שמואל: 'No secret is too hard for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with each sage praising the other. שמואל says רב was protected because he is a צדיק. רב says שמואל's knowledge is so broad that nothing is hidden from him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each one gives the other credit. רב was saved from harm even though he did not know about the danger, and שמואל was the one who knew how to spot and test it.

keyTerms.meaning: will not happen to, will not befall

steps.whatToRemember: A deer can be fully kosher by its signs and still be dangerous to eat because of a hidden snake bite. Being careful about health dangers is a separate concern from whether the animal is kosher.

phrases.english: Shmuel said this verse about Rav:
"No harm will happen to the righteous."
Rav said this verse about Shmuel:
"No secret is too hard for you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story after the test result in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב was protected because of his righteousness, and שמואל's wide knowledge uncovered the hidden danger.

steps.title: משנה: Torah signs for animals, Sages' signs for birds
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says the signs of kosher בהמה and חיה come from the Torah, but the Torah does not list signs for birds. So חכמים gave signs: a bird that claws its prey is not kosher, and a bird with an extra toe, a crop, and a gizzard whose lining peels off is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: The signs of a בהמה and a חיה were stated in the Torah. The signs of a bird were not stated. But חכמים said: any bird that claws its prey is not kosher. Any bird that has an extra toe, a crop, and a gizzard whose lining peels off is kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It explains where the kosher signs for animals and birds come from, and lists the signs חכמים gave for birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For animals the Torah itself gives the signs. For birds the Torah only lists the non-kosher kinds by name, so חכמים worked out signs to identify them. Clawing prey is a sign the bird is not kosher. The extra toe, the crop, and the peelable gizzard together are signs that it is kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: a bird that claws its prey and eats it
an extra toe, set back on the leg
crop, a pouch in the throat where food is stored

steps.confusionAlert: In this משנה, טמא and טהור mean not kosher and kosher to eat. They are not talking about ritual purity.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
The signs of a domesticated animal and a wild animal
phrases.notes: These are the signs that show the animal is kosher.

phrases.english: were stated in the Torah,
but the signs of a bird were not stated.
But the Sages said:
Any bird that claws its prey is not kosher.
Any bird that has an extra toe
and a crop, and whose gizzard lining peels off, is kosher.

steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָנֵי בְּהֵמָה וְחַיָּה נֶאֶמְרוּ מִן הַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on the signs of kosher creatures, after the story ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah gives the animal signs. חכמים gave the bird signs: clawing means not kosher; an extra toe, a crop, and a peelable gizzard mean kosher.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה is the base text for the whole discussion of kosher signs that follows.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק's sign for a non-kosher bird
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק adds another sign: any bird that splits its feet is not kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק says: Any bird that splits its feet is not kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: Another תנא in the משנה gives his own sign for recognizing a non-kosher bird.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clawing prey (step 11) is about how the bird eats. רבי אלעזר ברבי צדוק points to a physical sign instead: the way the bird spreads its feet.

keyTerms.meaning: splits its feet, spreads its toes apart

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, says:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל עוֹף הַחוֹלֵק אֶת רַגְלָיו – טָמֵא.
phrases.english: Any bird that splits its feet is not kosher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sign for a non-kosher bird beside the clawing sign of step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bird that splits its feet is not kosher.

steps.title: משנה: signs of kosher grasshoppers
steps.stepSummary: A kosher grasshopper has four legs, four wings, jumping legs, and wings that cover most of its body. רבי יוסי adds that its name must also be חגב.
steps.simpleTranslation: With grasshoppers: any that has four legs, four wings, jumping legs, and wings that cover most of its body is kosher. רבי יוסי says: and its name must be חגב.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves on to grasshoppers and lists the signs that make one kosher. רבי יוסי adds one more condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The physical signs are four legs, four wings, two jumping legs, and wings covering most of the body. רבי יוסי says the signs alone are not enough; the kind must also be known by the name חגב.

keyTerms.meaning: the jumping legs of a grasshopper

phrases.aramaic: וּבַחֲגָבִים, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אַרְבַּע רַגְלַיִם,
phrases.english: And with grasshoppers: any that has four legs,
and four wings, and jumping legs,
and whose wings cover most of its body.
phrases.notes: The משנה leaves it out, but it means such a grasshopper is kosher.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: And its name is "chagav."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבַחֲגָבִים, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אַרְבַּע רַגְלַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list, moving from birds to grasshoppers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A grasshopper with four legs, four wings, jumping legs, and wings covering most of its body is kosher; רבי יוסי also requires that its name be חגב.

steps.title: משנה: signs of kosher fish
steps.stepSummary: A kosher fish has a fin and a scale. רבי יהודה says it needs two scales and one fin. The משנה explains that scales are attached to the body and fins are what the fish swims with.
steps.simpleTranslation: With fish: any that has a fin and a scale is kosher. רבי יהודה says: two scales and one fin. Scales are the ones attached to it, and fins are the ones it swims with.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the signs of kosher fish, records רבי יהודה's view on the minimum amount, and explains what scales and fins are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says one fin and one scale are enough. רבי יהודה requires at least two scales and one fin. The ending defines the terms: scales are stuck onto the body, and fins are the parts the fish uses to swim.

keyTerms.meaning: the ones attached to its body
what it swims with, literally 'flies' with

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה gives signs for four groups: animals (from the Torah), birds and grasshoppers (from חכמים), and fish (fins and scales).

phrases.aramaic: וּבַדָּגִים, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ סְנַפִּיר וְקַשְׁקֶשֶׁת.
phrases.english: And with fish: any that has a fin and a scale is kosher.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
It needs two scales and one fin.
And these are scales: the ones attached to its body,
and fins are the ones it swims with.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּבַדָּגִים, כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ סְנַפִּיר וְקַשְׁקֶשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list, moving from grasshoppers to fish.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fish with a fin and a scale is kosher; רבי יהודה requires two scales and one fin. Scales are attached to the body; fins are used for swimming.

steps.title: ברייתא: signs of a kosher animal, and cud-chewers have no upper teeth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lists the Torah's signs for a kosher בהמה. It adds that any animal that chews its cud has no upper front teeth and is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: These are the signs of a בהמה: 'Any animal that has split hooves,' and so on. Any animal that chews its cud is known to have no upper teeth, and it is kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה's first line, that the Torah gives the signs of a kosher בהמה. It quotes a ברייתא that names the פסוק and adds a related fact about cud-chewing animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's signs are split hooves and chewing the cud. The ברייתא adds that every cud-chewing animal also lacks upper front teeth, so this feature goes together with being kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: a teaching of the תנאים not included in the משנה
upper teeth, the top front teeth

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ הֵן סִימָנֵי בְּהֵמָה –
phrases.english: The Sages taught: These are the signs of a domesticated animal:
"Any animal that has split hooves," and so on.
Any animal that chews its cud
is known for certain to have no upper teeth,
and it is kosher.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ הֵן סִימָנֵי בְּהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא on the משנה's statement in step 11 that the animal signs come from the Torah.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah's signs are split hooves and chewing the cud; any cud-chewing animal has no upper front teeth and is kosher.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a practical extra sign, missing upper teeth, that goes together with chewing the cud and helps identify a kosher animal.

steps.title: Is it really a rule? What about the camel?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's rule using the camel, which chews its cud and has no upper teeth, yet is not kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this really a rule? The camel chews its cud and has no upper teeth, and it is still not kosher!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the ברייתא from the last step. It brings the camel as an animal that seems to break the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא tied cud-chewing, having no upper teeth, and being kosher together. The camel chews its cud and seems to have no upper teeth, but the Torah calls it not kosher. So 'no upper teeth' cannot be a reliable sign of a kosher animal.

keyTerms.meaning: A general rule that always holds

phrases.english: And is this a fixed rule?
But there is the camel, which chews its cud,
and has no upper teeth, and it is not kosher!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the teeth rule from the ברייתא in step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a cud-chewing animal has no upper teeth and is kosher
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The camel fits the signs (chews its cud, no upper teeth) but the Torah says it is not kosher

steps.title: The camel has side teeth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a camel does have upper side teeth, so it does not count as an animal with no upper teeth.
steps.simpleTranslation: A camel has tusk-like side teeth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the camel question. A camel does have some upper teeth, so it does not break the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule speaks about an animal with no upper teeth at all. The camel has two tusk-like teeth on top, one on each side. So it is not really an exception.

phrases.english: A camel has tusk-like teeth.
phrases.notes: These are upper teeth on each side, so the camel does have some upper teeth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the camel challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual correction: the camel does have upper teeth
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The camel has no upper teeth at all
steps.terutzMaskana: The camel has tusk-like upper teeth, so the rule holds

steps.title: Three more problems: the young camel, the שפן and ארנבת, and the Torah's silence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks three more questions: a young camel has no side teeth at all; the שפן and ארנבת chew their cud but have upper teeth; and the Torah never mentions teeth.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a young camel doesn't even have the side teeth, and it is not kosher! And also, the שפן and ארנבת chew their cud and do have upper teeth, and they are not kosher! And besides, does the Torah write anything about teeth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes harder against the rule. It gives three separate problems, one after the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, a young camel has no upper teeth at all, but it is still not kosher. Second, the שפן and ארנבת chew their cud yet have upper teeth, so 'every cud-chewer has no upper teeth' is wrong. Third, the Torah lists signs for kosher animals and teeth are not one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Hyrax, a cud-chewing animal that is not kosher
Hare, a cud-chewing animal that is not kosher
And further / and besides: adding more challenges

phrases.english: But there is the young camel,
which does not even have the tusk-like teeth,
And further, there are the hyrax and the hare,
which chew their cud
and do have upper teeth, and they are not kosher!
And besides, are teeth written in the Torah?

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲרֵי בֶּן גָּמָל, דְּנִיבֵי נָמֵי לֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the camel answer by bringing the young camel, then adds two more challenges
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule linking cud-chewing and having no upper teeth
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The young camel has no upper teeth and is not kosher; the שפן and ארנבת chew their cud but have upper teeth; and teeth are never mentioned in the Torah

steps.title: Reading the rule the other way around
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: it does not say every cud-chewer lacks upper teeth. It says that an animal with no upper teeth surely chews its cud, has split hooves, and is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what the ברייתא means: any animal that has no upper teeth surely chews its cud and has split hooves, and it is kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by flipping the direction of the rule. Missing upper teeth is a clue that tells you the animal has the Torah's real signs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שפן and ארנבת are no longer a problem, because the rule doesn't claim every cud-chewer lacks teeth; it only starts from 'no upper teeth'. Teeth are not a new Torah sign; they are just a way to know that the Torah's signs are there. The young camel is still a problem, and the גמרא handles it in step 23.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what it means: rereading a source

steps.confusionAlert: The rule now starts from the teeth, not from chewing the cud. It no longer claims that every cud-chewer lacks upper teeth (the שפן and ארנבת have them). It only says that an animal with no upper teeth has the Torah's signs and is kosher.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it is saying:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל בְּהֵמָה שֶׁאֵין לָהּ שִׁינַּיִם לְמַעְלָה –
phrases.english: Any animal that has no upper teeth,
it is certain that it chews its cud
and has split hooves, and is kosher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenges by rereading the ברייתא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source (reversing the direction of the rule)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every cud-chewing animal has no upper teeth
steps.terutzMaskana: Every animal with no upper teeth has the Torah's signs and is kosher

steps.title: Why not just check the hooves?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we need a teeth test at all. Just look at the hooves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him just check its hooves!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the teeth sign is for. The Torah's own sign, split hooves, is easy to see.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the teeth only show that the Torah's signs are present, why not check those signs directly? The hooves are right there to look at.

phrases.english: Let him check its hooves!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the need for the rule as it was reread in step 19
steps.kashyaTarget: The usefulness of the teeth sign
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah's hoof sign can be checked directly, so the teeth sign seems pointless

steps.title: When the hooves are cut off: רב חסדא's desert case
steps.stepSummary: The teeth sign is needed when the hooves are cut off. רב חסדא rules that someone who finds such an animal in the desert checks its mouth, as long as he can recognize a camel.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed when the hooves were cut off, like רב חסדא said: if someone was walking in the desert and found an animal with cut-off hooves, he checks its mouth. If it has no upper teeth, it is surely kosher. If it does, it is surely not kosher. This is only if he can recognize a camel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains when the teeth test is used: when you can't see the hooves. It brings רב חסדא's ruling as an example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the hooves cut off, the Torah's hoof sign can't be checked, so the mouth becomes the test. רב חסדא adds a condition: you must be able to recognize a camel, since a camel has no front upper teeth and is not kosher. The next step will question this condition.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical way to know if an animal is kosher when the Torah's sign can't be seen.

phrases.english: For example, where its hooves were cut off,
and this is like Rav Chisda,
for Rav Chisda said:
If someone was walking in the desert
and found an animal whose hooves were cut off,
he checks its mouth.
If it has no upper teeth,
it is certain that it is kosher;
if not, it is certain that it is not kosher,
as long as he recognizes a camel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the hooves can't just be checked
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule to a special case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The hooves can always be checked
steps.terutzMaskana: The teeth test is for when the hooves are cut off, as רב חסדא ruled

steps.title: But the camel has side teeth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב חסדא needs to warn about a camel, since a camel has upper side teeth anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a camel has tusk-like teeth!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions רב חסדא's condition. A camel would fail the teeth test anyway, so why mention it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 said a camel has upper side teeth. So a camel would not pass the 'no upper teeth' test, and there is nothing to warn about.

phrases.english: But a camel has tusk-like teeth!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the camel condition in רב חסדא's ruling
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'as long as he recognizes a camel'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A camel has upper side teeth, so it would never be mistaken for kosher by this test

steps.title: Read it as 'a young camel'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the condition: he must be able to recognize a young camel, which really has no upper teeth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, read it: as long as he recognizes a young camel.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes רב חסדא's condition so it makes sense. The danger is a young camel, not a grown one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A young camel has no upper teeth at all (step 18), so it would pass the teeth test even though it is not kosher. That is why the person must be able to recognize it. This also takes care of the young camel problem from step 18.

phrases.english: Rather, as long as he recognizes a young camel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers by correcting the wording of רב חסדא's condition
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The condition was about a grown camel
steps.terutzMaskana: The condition is about a young camel, which has no upper teeth

steps.title: Maybe another animal looks like a young camel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the young camel is an exception, maybe there are other unknown animals like it, so the teeth test can't be trusted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't you say there is a young camel? Maybe there is also another kind of animal that is like a young camel!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא worries the teeth test is still not safe. If one exception exists, there may be others we don't know about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we admit that one non-kosher animal has no upper teeth, how can we rely on the mouth at all? There may be another species that also has no upper teeth and is not kosher.

phrases.english: Didn't you say there is a young camel?
Maybe there is also another kind
that is like a young camel!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reliability of רב חסדא's teeth test
steps.kashyaTarget: Relying on the mouth test in רב חסדא's case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If one exception exists, other unknown exceptions may exist too

steps.title: Only the camel: proof from the word הוּא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the worry with a teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל: the word הוּא in the פסוק shows that the camel is the only animal that chews its cud and is not kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'And the camel, because it chews its cud'. The Ruler of His world knows that there is nothing that chews its cud and is not kosher except the camel. So the פסוק singled it out with the word 'הוּא'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that there is no other animal like the young camel. It proves this from the extra word הוּא in the פסוק about the camel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only ה׳, who rules the world, could know every species, and the Torah tells us the camel is unique by saying הוּא, meaning 'it and no other'. So no other unknown animal will fool the teeth test. The only exception to watch for is the camel itself, including a young one.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't think that; that idea is wrong
The Ruler of His world, ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: An animal with no upper front teeth is kosher. This test is used when the hooves are cut off, and you only need to watch out for a young camel. The Torah's word הוּא shows the camel is the only animal like this.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the Torah's list of non-kosher animals is complete, so a sign like this can be trusted.

phrases.english: Don't think that,
for the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"And the camel, because it chews its cud",
The Ruler of His world knows

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ דָּבָר מַעֲלֵה גֵרָה וְטָמֵא אֶלָּא גָּמָל,
phrases.english: that there is nothing that chews its cud and is not kosher except the camel.
Therefore the verse singled it out with "it".

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ, דְּתָנֵי דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry about unknown species with a proof from a פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There may be other unknown animals like the young camel
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah tells us the camel is the only cud-chewing animal that is not kosher
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The teeth test is reliable as long as one recognizes a young camel

steps.title: רב חסדא: When the mouth is damaged, check the hooves
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that if you find an animal with a damaged mouth, you check its hooves. Split hooves mean it is kosher, as long as you can recognize a חזיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: If someone was traveling and found an animal whose mouth was cut off, he checks its hooves. If the hooves are split, it is definitely kosher. If not, it is definitely not kosher. This only works if he knows what a pig looks like.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a new rule. When you cannot check the animal's teeth, you can rely on its hooves instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the teeth were used as the sign. Here the mouth is damaged, so the teeth cannot be checked, and the hooves become the test. There is one exception to watch for: the חזיר has split hooves but is not kosher. So the test only works for someone who can tell a pig apart from other animals.

keyTerms.meaning: cut off or damaged (here: the mouth)
as long as, on condition that

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda says:
If one was walking on the road
and he found an animal whose mouth was cut off,
he checks its hooves:
if its hooves are split,
it is certainly kosher;
if not, it is certainly not kosher,
provided that he recognizes a pig.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הָיָה מְהַלֵּךְ בַּדֶּרֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling of רב חסדא: after the teeth test (with the camel exception), here is the hoof test (with the pig exception).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An animal with a damaged mouth is identified by its hooves. Split hooves mean it is kosher, as long as the person can recognize a חזיר.

steps.title: Maybe other animals are like the pig
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if the pig is an exception, maybe there are other unknown animals like it, which would make the hoof test unreliable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't you just say there is a pig, which has split hooves and is still not kosher? Then maybe there is another kind of animal like the pig too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the hoof test. It asks the same question it asked about the camel in step 24.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even one animal with split hooves can be non-kosher, how can we be sure the pig is the only one? An unknown look-alike would break the rule that split hooves mean kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: that resembles, that is similar to

phrases.english: Didn't you say there is a pig?
There may also be another species
that is similar to a pig!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reliability of רב חסדא's hoof test.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that split hooves prove an animal is kosher.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since one exception (the pig) exists, there could be other unknown exceptions, so the sign cannot be trusted.

steps.title: The word הוּא shows the pig is the only exception
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל: the word הוּא in the פסוק shows that the pig is the only animal with split hooves that is not kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't think that. The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: the verse says 'And the pig, because it splits the hoof, it is...' God, who rules His world, knows that nothing splits the hoof and is not kosher except the pig. That is why the verse singles it out with the word 'it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the worry by showing from the תורה that there is no other animal like the pig.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word הוּא ("it") points to the pig alone. God knows every animal in the world, so if the תורה singles out the pig, no other animal can have split hooves and still be non-kosher. This answer follows the same pattern used for the camel in step 25.

keyTerms.meaning: don't think that, it can't be

steps.whatToRemember: The pig is the only animal with split hooves that is not kosher. So for anyone who can recognize a pig, split hooves are a reliable sign.

phrases.english: Don't think so,
for the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
"And the pig, because it splits the hoof, it"
The Ruler of His world knows

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁמַּפְרִיס פַּרְסָה וְטָמֵא
phrases.english: that there is nothing that splits the hoof and is not kosher
except the pig;
therefore the verse singled it out with "it."

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ, דְּתָנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about pig-like animals.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Scriptural proof that the exception is unique
steps.terutzHavaAmina: There could be other unknown animals with split hooves that are not kosher.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word הוּא shows that the pig is the only one, so the hoof test is reliable.

steps.title: רב חסדא: When mouth and hooves are both damaged, check the flesh
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that if both the mouth and the hooves are damaged, you check the flesh. If it runs in crisscross directions, the animal is kosher, as long as you can recognize an ערוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא also said: If someone was traveling in the desert and found an animal whose mouth was cut off and whose hooves were cut off, he checks its flesh. If the flesh runs lengthwise and crosswise, it is definitely kosher. If not, it is definitely not kosher. This only works if he knows what a wild donkey looks like.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא gives a third test, for when neither the teeth nor the hooves can be checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With both of the usual signs missing, the flesh itself becomes the test. Kosher animals have flesh whose fibers run in two directions, like threads in woven cloth. The ערוד also has flesh like this but is not kosher, so the person must be able to recognize it.

phrases.english: And Rav Chisda says:
If one was walking in the desert,
and he found an animal whose mouth was cut off
and whose hooves were cut off,
he checks its flesh,
if it runs lengthwise and crosswise,
phrases.notes: Picture woven cloth: some threads run up and down and some run across.

phrases.english: it is certainly kosher;
and if not, it is certainly not kosher,
provided that he recognizes a wild donkey.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: הָיָה מְהַלֵּךְ בַּמִּדְבָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third parallel ruling of רב חסדא, for when both earlier signs are missing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When both mouth and hooves are damaged, flesh running lengthwise and crosswise shows the animal is kosher, as long as the person can recognize an ערוד.

steps.title: Maybe other animals are like the wild donkey
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: if the ערוד is an exception, maybe there is another unknown animal like it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't you say there is a wild donkey, whose flesh runs both ways and is still not kosher? Then maybe there is another kind of animal like it too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question it asked about the pig, this time about the flesh test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One known exception raises the worry that there are unknown exceptions. If such an animal existed, the flesh test could not be trusted.

phrases.english: Didn't you say there is a wild donkey?
There may also be another species
that is similar to a wild donkey!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reliability of the flesh test.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that crisscross flesh proves an animal is kosher.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the ערוד is an exception, there could be other unknown exceptions.

steps.title: A tradition says there is no other animal like it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there is a received tradition that no other animal is like the ערוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a tradition that there is none.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the worry by relying on a tradition passed down from earlier teachers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time there is no פסוק to quote, as there was for the pig. Instead the answer rests on a tradition that the ערוד is the only exception, so the flesh test stays reliable.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a פסוק here. Unlike the pig, the proof is a tradition (גמירי), not a verse.

phrases.english: It is learned as a tradition that there is none.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about animals that look like the ערוד.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Other unknown animals might have flesh like the ערוד.
steps.terutzMaskana: Tradition says there are none, so the flesh test is reliable.

steps.title: Where on the body is the flesh checked?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where on the animal one checks the flesh.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where does he check?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about how to carry out the flesh test. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא said to check the flesh but did not say where. The גמרא wants to know the exact spot.

phrases.english: And where does he check?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for practical details about רב חסדא's flesh test.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact place on the body where the flesh is examined.

steps.title: Check at the area by the tailbone
steps.stepSummary: אביי (or some say רב חסדא) answers that the flesh is checked at the sides of the tailbone.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said, and some say it was רב חסדא: at the sides of the tailbone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer: the place to check is the flesh near the tailbone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer names a specific spot, the flesh at the edges of the tailbone, where the crisscross pattern can be seen. There are two versions of who said it.
steps.whatToRemember: רב חסדא gave three backup tests. If the mouth is damaged, check the hooves (but watch for the pig). If the hooves are damaged, check the teeth (but watch for the young camel). If both are damaged, check the flesh near the tailbone (but watch for the wild donkey).

phrases.english: Abaye said, and some say Rav Chisda:
At the sides of the tailbone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about where to check.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The flesh is checked at the sides of the tailbone.

steps.title: The signs of an undomesticated animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's phrase 'the signs of a חיה' and brings a ברייתא that begins listing them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה mentioned the signs of a חיה. Our Rabbis taught in a ברייתא: These are the signs of a חיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה, the signs of a kosher חיה, and opens a ברייתא that is about to list them. This line sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion was about a בהמה (a domesticated animal). Now the topic switches to a חיה, a wild animal like a deer. The ברייתא's opening words, 'these are the signs,' suggest that a חיה has its own separate signs.

keyTerms.meaning: The signs that show a wild animal is kosher
An undomesticated or wild animal, such as a deer
A teaching from the time of the משנה that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: The signs of an undomesticated animal.
The Rabbis taught:
These are the signs of an undomesticated animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָנֵי חַיָּה. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵלּוּ הֵן סִימָנֵי חַיָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of checking a בהמה's flesh (Step 33) and starts the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a ברייתא that lists the signs of a kosher חיה.

steps.title: Why does a wild animal need its own signs?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא: a חיה is already included under בהמה for the signs, so why list separate signs for it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But a חיה is included in the category of בהמה regarding signs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops right after the ברייתא's opening line and challenges it. If the Torah already treats a חיה like a בהמה for kosher signs, why does it need a list of its own?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah gives the signs (split hooves and chewing the cud) for a בהמה, and the פסוק includes a חיה in that same group. So a חיה should be kosher by those same two signs. A separate list for a חיה looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: A domesticated animal, such as a cow or sheep
Signs, here the signs that show an animal is kosher

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether a חיה is kosher. It is why a חיה would need different signs, if the Torah already treats it like a בהמה for kosher signs.

phrases.english: An undomesticated animal is included in the category of domesticated animal
phrases.notes: This comes from ויקרא 11:2–3, where the פסוק says חיה and then בהמה together before giving the signs.

phrases.english: with regard to signs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ברייתא quoted in Step 34.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that there are separate signs for a חיה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Torah includes a חיה under בהמה for the kosher signs, so a separate list of signs for a חיה seems unnecessary.

steps.title: רבי זירא begins his answer
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא starts to answer why a חיה needs its own signs. His words continue on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only opens רבי זירא's answer to the question. The actual answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is said yet. We only learn that the answer will come from רבי זירא, and that it will explain what the separate signs of a חיה are for.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the challenge raised in Step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The answer has not been given yet; it continues on the next amud.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a חיה is included under בהמה for signs, a separate list for it seems unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Still to come: רבי זירא will explain what the separate signs of a חיה are for.
